## 9.4 Thermal control system

*[Source: ECSS-E-ST-31C; Gilmore, Ch. 1–4; SMAD, Ch. 11.5]*

Figure 9.5 summarises the energy balance this section develops: four heat inputs (direct solar, Earth albedo, Earth infrared and the spacecraft's own electrical dissipation) and a single output, radiation to deep space, with the hot- and cold-case conditions that bound the design.

![Thermal energy-balance schematic of a CubeSat in LEO with solar, albedo, Earth-IR and internal inputs, radiation to space, and hot-case and cold-case annotations.](../assets/figures/fig_thermal_schematic.png)

**Figure 9.5** — Thermal energy balance of a CubeSat in LEO. Direct solar flux, Earth albedo and Earth infrared are absorbed according to the coating properties <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the view factors; internal dissipation adds the electrical power converted to heat; the only outlet is radiation to deep space, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0c50d80e2c0a06af.svg" alt="\varepsilon \sigma A_{\text{rad}} T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The hot case combines perihelion Sun, maximum dissipation, end-of-life coatings and maximum albedo; the cold case is eclipse in safe mode with beginning-of-life coatings and minimum Earth infrared (§9.4.5).

### 9.4.1 The physics of spacecraft thermal control

Spacecraft thermal control is fundamentally different from terrestrial thermal engineering because **there is no convection in vacuum**. The only heat transfer mechanisms are:

1. **Conduction:** Heat flow through solid material, governed by Fourier's law: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_413fdbea9434f006.svg" alt="\dot{Q} = -kA \dfrac{dT}{dx}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. Critical within the spacecraft structure and between components and mounting surfaces.
2. **Radiation:** Heat transfer via electromagnetic radiation, governed by the Stefan–Boltzmann law: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2294c48d26e11183.svg" alt="\dot{Q} = \varepsilon \sigma A T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. This is the **only** mechanism for rejecting heat to the environment.

There is no convective cooling. A component that overheats cannot be cooled by a fan. All waste heat must be conducted to a radiating surface and then radiated to space. This is the central constraint of spacecraft thermal design.

### 9.4.2 Thermal environment in LEO

A spacecraft in LEO experiences four thermal inputs and one thermal sink:

| Source | Flux | Direction | Variability |
|--------|------|-----------|-------------|
| **Direct solar** | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c80cf3902a852e75.svg" alt="S = 1361 \pm 1" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² (at 1 AU) | Sun-facing surfaces only | Seasonal (±3.3 % due to Earth's orbital eccentricity: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_30bb4894144607bf.svg" alt="S_{\text{perihelion}} = 1414" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² in January, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d5886d49956f187b.svg" alt="S_{\text{aphelion}} = 1322" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² in July) |
| **Earth albedo** | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_eee8b13741dd02e7.svg" alt="\alpha_E \times S \approx 0.30 \times 1361 \approx 408" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² | Earth-facing surfaces (nadir) | Varies with cloud cover, surface type (0.06 for ocean to 0.80 for fresh snow); orbit-average range 0.25–0.35 |
| **Earth infrared** | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2e75b691f649c2cc.svg" alt="q_{\text{IR}} \approx 240" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² (orbit average) | Earth-facing surfaces (nadir) | Range 200–270 W/m² depending on latitude, season, cloud cover |
| **Internal dissipation** | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f2a341396f5760a9.svg" alt="Q_{\text{int}} = P_{\text{dissipated}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | From electronics waste heat | Varies with operational mode; nearly all electrical power eventually becomes heat |
| **Deep space** (sink) | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fb42cc7d481cbbd5.svg" alt="T_{\text{space}} \approx 2.7" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K (CMB) | Zenith-facing radiator surfaces | Effectively 0 K for engineering purposes |

### 9.4.3 View factors

The fraction of a surface's radiative "view" that sees each thermal source is critical for accurate thermal modelling. For a flat nadir-facing surface in LEO:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_02709b08a419b64e.svg" alt="F_{\text{Earth}} = \frac{1}{1 + (h/R_E)^2 + 2(h/R_E)} = \left(\frac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the altitude and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bd32146d65fed1e1.svg" alt="R_E = 6378.137" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km. For a 500 km orbit: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a9e52ab9c21f27a0.svg" alt="F_{\text{Earth}} = (6378.137/6878.137)^2 = 0.860" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The nadir face sees 86 % Earth and 14 % deep space. The zenith face sees 100 % deep space (assuming no self-shadowing). Side faces see a mix.

At higher altitudes <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8f71e4d2a4a5ce96.svg" alt="F_{\text{Earth}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> decreases: at 800 km it is 0.79, at 35 786 km (GEO) it is only 0.023 — which is why GEO thermal design is dominated by solar flux and internal dissipation, not Earth IR and albedo.

### 9.4.4 Thermal balance equation

> **Key equations — thermal equilibrium** (Part V §V.10)
>
> At steady state, the absorbed heat equals the radiated heat:
> 

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_610c499dfe9c926c.svg" alt="Q_{\text{in}} = Q_{\text{out}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>


>
> **Absorbed heat (expanded):**
> 

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2ebcd51491e47445.svg" alt="Q_{\text{in}} = \underbrace{\alpha_s \cdot A_{\text{sun}} \cdot S}_{\text{direct solar}} + \underbrace{\alpha_s \cdot A_{\text{alb}} \cdot F_{\text{alb}} \cdot \alpha_E \cdot S}_{\text{Earth albedo}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon \cdot A_{\text{IR}} \cdot F_{\text{IR}} \cdot q_{\text{IR}}}_{\text{Earth IR}} + \underbrace{Q_{\text{int}}}_{\text{internal dissipation}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>


>
> **Radiated heat:**
> 

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_87bb25b77ab5a180.svg" alt="Q_{\text{out}} = \varepsilon \cdot \sigma \cdot A_{\text{rad}} \cdot T^4" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>


>
> where:
>
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> = solar absorptance of surface coating (dimensionless, 0–1)
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> = infrared emittance of surface coating (dimensionless, 0–1)
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2d0c8f6a914c71d3.svg" alt="\sigma = 5.670 \times 10^{-8}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m²/K⁴ (Stefan–Boltzmann constant)
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1cbb2f0cce436717.svg" alt="A_{\text{sun}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_93e068d7745a9f31.svg" alt="A_{\text{alb}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8010644418cec707.svg" alt="A_{\text{IR}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4fcb34f4471e4f1d.svg" alt="A_{\text{rad}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> = projected areas for each flux (m²)
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_512e994cc198cf39.svg" alt="F_{\text{alb}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0cdc5c63a5ba8ccb.svg" alt="F_{\text{IR}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> = view factors to Earth for albedo and IR surfaces
> - <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5f8eb8cbe0662591.svg" alt="T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> = equilibrium temperature (K)
>
> **Note on <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> vs <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:** Solar absorptance (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) is measured over the solar spectrum (0.2–2.5 µm, peak at 0.5 µm visible). Infrared emittance (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) is measured over the thermal IR spectrum (3–50 µm, peak at ~10 µm for room-temperature objects). These are **different spectral ranges**, so <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ac4e2275cd3e2a0c.svg" alt="\alpha_s \neq \varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> for most real surfaces. This decoupling is the basis of all passive thermal control: by choosing the <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> ratio, the designer controls the equilibrium temperature.
>
> **Solving for equilibrium temperature:**
> 

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a769f86b302084fa.svg" alt="T = \left(\frac{Q_{\text{absorbed}} + Q_{\text{internal}}}{\varepsilon \sigma A_{\text{rad}}}\right)^{1/4}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>


>
> This equation is valid only for a single isothermal node (lumped-parameter model). For multi-node thermal models (needed for any real spacecraft), the heat balance is solved simultaneously for all nodes using numerical thermal-analysis software.

### 9.4.5 Hot case and cold case

| Case | Conditions | Design concern |
|------|-----------|----------------|
| **Hot case** | Maximum solar exposure (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4162c8d4c5985d7f.svg" alt="S = 1414" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m², perihelion), all subsystems active (max <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0ed87e80e6e0e126.svg" alt="Q_{\text{int}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>), worst Sun angle (max <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1cbb2f0cce436717.svg" alt="A_{\text{sun}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>), EOL coatings (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> increased by UV darkening), max albedo (0.35) | Components exceed maximum operating temperature |
| **Cold case** | Eclipse (no solar), minimum power dissipation (safe mode, min <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0ed87e80e6e0e126.svg" alt="Q_{\text{int}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>), BOL coatings (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at its lowest), minimum Earth IR (200 W/m²), deep-space view | Components fall below minimum operating temperature |

**Design philosophy:** The thermal engineer designs to keep all components within their qualified temperature range under both worst-case hot and worst-case cold conditions, with ECSS-mandated margins applied.

### 9.4.6 Surface coatings — the passive thermal toolbox

| Coating | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (BOL) | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (EOL, 5 yr LEO) | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (BOL) | Use case |
|---------|-----------|---------------------------|--------------|------------------------|----------|
| White paint (AZ-93, S13G-LO) | 0.14–0.20 | 0.25–0.35 | 0.89–0.92 | 0.16–0.22 | Radiator surfaces (stay cool; low solar absorption, high IR emission) |
| Black paint (Aeroglaze Z306) | 0.95 | 0.95 | 0.89 | 1.07 | Internal surfaces (maximise radiative exchange between components) |
| Gold tape (2 mil Kapton + VDA) | 0.22–0.25 | 0.25–0.30 | 0.03–0.05 | 5.0–7.5 | MLI outer layer, thermal isolation |
| Bare aluminium (polished) | 0.10–0.15 | 0.15–0.20 | 0.03–0.05 | 2.5–4.0 | Reflective surfaces, low emissivity |
| Alodine (chromate conversion on Al) | 0.35–0.40 | 0.40–0.50 | 0.12–0.16 | 2.5–3.0 | Moderate thermal control, structural surfaces |
| Anodised aluminium (clear or black) | 0.30–0.50 | 0.35–0.55 | 0.75–0.86 | 0.4–0.65 | CubeSat external structure (standard finish per CDS) |
| MLI blanket (effective) | 0.05–0.15 | 0.10–0.20 | 0.02–0.05 | ~3 | Thermal isolation of sensitive components |
| Solar cells (with cover glass) | 0.75–0.92 | 0.78–0.92 | 0.80–0.85 | ~1.0 | SA surfaces (high absorption is unavoidable; cells get hot) |
| OSR (Optical Solar Reflector) | 0.05–0.08 | 0.08–0.12 | 0.78–0.80 | 0.06–0.10 | High-performance radiators (large S/C, GEO) |

**Key design insight:** A surface with low <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (e.g., white paint: 0.2) stays cool because it reflects most solar energy but efficiently radiates thermal IR. A surface with high <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (e.g., gold tape: 6.0) stays warm because it absorbs solar energy but barely radiates. This is why white paint is used on radiators and gold or MLI for insulation. Figure 9.6 plots the equilibrium temperature of a flat plate in LEO against this ratio.

![Radiative thermal equilibrium versus α/ε.](../assets/figures/fig_thermal_balance.png)

**Figure 9.6** — Orbit-average equilibrium temperature of a flat plate in LEO as a function of <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, with common coatings marked. White paint sits well below the electronics operating band, black paint near its upper edge; the dashed line is the eclipse-only (no Sun) temperature.

**Coating degradation:** UV radiation darkens most white paints over time, increasing <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> while leaving <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> nearly unchanged. The ratio <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> therefore rises, and the surface runs hotter at EOL. The consequence for worst-case analysis is easy to get backwards: BOL white paint has the *lowest* <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, so the **cold case is most conservative with BOL properties**, while the **hot case is most conservative with EOL properties** after <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_369c9c210487d0c9.svg" alt="\alpha_s" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> has increased. Both cases must be run with the properties that make them worst.

### 9.4.7 MLI (multi-layer insulation) — construction and physics

MLI blankets are the most common thermal insulation on spacecraft. They work by minimising both radiation and conduction heat transfer through multiple reflective layers separated by low-conductance spacers.

**Construction (typical MLI blanket):**

1. **Outer cover:** 1 mil (25 µm) aluminised Kapton (VDA — vapour-deposited aluminium on one side). Provides mechanical protection and low solar absorptance.
2. **Inner reflective layers:** 10–20 layers of 0.25 mil (6 µm) double-aluminised Mylar (DAM). Each layer reflects IR radiation, and the vacuum gaps between layers have zero convection.
3. **Spacer material:** Dacron or Nomex netting between each DAM layer, preventing conductive contact between adjacent reflective sheets.
4. **Inner cover:** 1 mil aluminised Kapton, protecting the inner layers.

**Effective emissivity:** An ideal MLI blanket with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7a46d47ab4f491f7.svg" alt="N" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> reflective layers has an effective emissivity of:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b9048d1bcf945253.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} = \frac{1}{2/\varepsilon_{\text{inner}} + (N-1)(2/\varepsilon_{\text{layer}} - 1)}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



For 20 layers of DAM (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ca08c46622aeee91.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{layer}} = 0.03" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9a39f615d304e073.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} \approx 0.002" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. In practice, real MLI achieves <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bc60029f067c4143.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} = 0.01" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>–<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7d7ef6eb96ec1cc3.svg" alt="0.03" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> due to seams, penetrations (harness, mounting) and edge effects. The ratio of actual to theoretical performance is typically 2–5× worse.

**CubeSat MLI challenges:** CubeSats have limited surface area and many penetrations (connectors, antennas, sensors, solar cells), making it difficult to achieve good MLI performance. Most CubeSats in LEO do not use MLI — they rely on the moderate thermal environment (Earth IR provides a "warm floor") and surface coatings. MLI becomes essential for deep-space CubeSats (e.g., MarCO, CAPSTONE) or missions with sensitive payloads (IR detectors, laser systems).

### 9.4.8 Heater sizing

When passive thermal control cannot prevent a component from falling below its minimum temperature (typically during eclipse or safe mode), electrical heaters are required.

> **Key equations — heater sizing**
>
> **Required heater power** (to maintain minimum temperature during the worst cold case):
> 

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5cdbf25fc3312414.svg" alt="P_{\text{heater}} = \varepsilon \sigma A_{\text{rad}} T_{\text{min}}^4 - Q_{\text{environment,cold}} - Q_{\text{internal,cold}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>


> where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d99e3c4296e92832.svg" alt="T_{\text{min}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the minimum allowable temperature of the component (in kelvin).
>
> **Heater types for CubeSats:**
>
> - **Kapton foil heaters:** Etched-foil resistance elements laminated between Kapton sheets. Flexible, thin (0.2–0.5 mm), lightweight (2–10 g each). Typical power 0.5–5 W per heater. Bond directly to the component surface with pressure-sensitive adhesive.
> - **Cartridge heaters:** Cylindrical, inserted into drilled holes. Higher power density but heavier and less common on CubeSats.
>
> **Thermostat control:** Simple bimetallic thermostats switch heaters on/off at set temperatures (e.g., on at −5 °C, off at +5 °C). Mass ~2 g each. For higher reliability, software-controlled heaters using temperature-sensor feedback and EPS switches are preferred on modern CubeSats — but this requires the OBC to be running, which may not be the case in safe mode.

### 9.4.9 Heat pipes and thermal straps

**Heat pipes** are passive two-phase heat-transfer devices that transport large amounts of thermal energy with very small temperature differences. They are widely used on larger spacecraft and are beginning to appear on 6U+ CubeSats.

**How a heat pipe works:**

1. Working fluid (ammonia, methanol, or water) evaporates at the hot end (evaporator), absorbing latent heat
2. Vapour travels through the hollow pipe core to the cold end (condenser)
3. At the condenser, vapour releases latent heat and condenses back to liquid
4. Liquid returns to the evaporator via capillary action in a wick structure (sintered metal, axial grooves, or screen mesh)
5. The process is continuous, passive (no moving parts, no power), and can transport 10–100 W across 20–50 cm with < 5 °C temperature difference

**Thermal conductance of a heat pipe:** Effective thermal conductivity is 10 000–100 000 W/m/K (compared with copper at 400 W/m/K and aluminium at 237 W/m/K). A 6 mm diameter ammonia heat pipe can transport ~30 W over 30 cm with < 3 °C gradient.

**Thermal straps** are flexible conductive links (braided copper, graphite fibre, or pyrolytic graphite sheet) used to conduct heat between components that cannot be rigidly connected (e.g., across a hinge or between a vibration-isolated payload and the spacecraft bus). Typical conductance: 0.5–5 W/K.

| Heat transport method | Conductance | Mass | Power | Orientation sensitivity | CubeSat use |
|----------------------|-------------|------|-------|------------------------|------------|
| Aluminium conduction | ~0.5–2 W/K per path | Part of structure | 0 W | None | Always (inherent) |
| Copper thermal strap | 1–5 W/K | 10–50 g | 0 W | None | Occasional (6U+) |
| Heat pipe (ammonia) | 5–50 W/K | 20–100 g | 0 W | Gravity-dependent (must test in relevant orientation) | Rare (6U+, some 3U) |
| Pumped fluid loop | 50–500 W/K | 500+ g | 5–20 W | None | Large S/C only |

### 9.4.10 Thermal control methods summary

| Method | Type | Mass impact | Typical use | Key design parameter |
|--------|------|-------------|------------|---------------------|
| **Surface coatings** | Passive | Negligible | Always — select <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> ratio per face | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> ratio |
| **MLI blankets** | Passive | 0.5–2.0 kg/m² | Insulate sensitive components from environment | Number of layers, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fed04749605a005e.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> |
| **Radiators** | Passive | Part of structure | Reject internal waste heat to deep space | Radiator area, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f3ab155c49d5e147.svg" alt="\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, view to space |
| **Heaters** | Active | 0.005–0.02 kg each | Maintain minimum temperature during eclipse/safe mode | Power, thermostat set point |
| **Heat pipes** | Passive | 0.02–0.10 kg each | Transport heat from source to radiator | Working fluid, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_92fe3fc15a6eb16a.svg" alt="Q_{\text{max}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, orientation |
| **Thermal straps** | Passive | 0.01–0.05 kg each | Flexible conductive link across joints/hinges | Conductance (W/K) |
| **Louvres** | Active | 0.1–0.5 kg | Variable-conductance radiators (rare on CubeSats) | Open/close temperature range |

### 9.4.11 ECSS thermal margins

*[Source: ECSS-E-ST-31C, Table 5-1]*

| Level | Hot margin (above predicted max) | Cold margin (below predicted min) |
|-------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Qualification** | Predicted + 15 °C | Predicted − 15 °C |
| **Acceptance** | Predicted + 10 °C | Predicted − 10 °C |
| **Operating** | Predicted + 5 °C | Predicted − 5 °C |

These margins ensure that thermal-model uncertainties (typically ±5–10 °C for simplified models, ±2–5 °C for detailed correlated models) do not cause in-orbit temperature exceedances.

> **Worked example — EOSat-3U single-node thermal analysis**
>
> **Hot case (sunlit, peak mode, perihelion, EOL coatings):**
>
> Simplified single-node model. 3U CubeSat, nadir-pointing.
>
> - Sun-facing area (+Z, zenith-facing 3U panel): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f5fe318df90b72fd.svg" alt="A_{\text{sun}} = 0.034" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m²
> - SA surfaces (Sun-facing): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d5096f2ab3498f72.svg" alt="\alpha_s = 0.85" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4d06e24ef40fab3f.svg" alt="\varepsilon = 0.82" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (solar-cell properties)
> - Nadir face (−Z): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_456ec2a8d08f8ee4.svg" alt="A_{\text{nadir}} = 0.034" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m², anodised Al (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3efb137f0b02ab48.svg" alt="\alpha_s = 0.45" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> EOL, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4d06e24ef40fab3f.svg" alt="\varepsilon = 0.82" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>)
> - Side faces (4×): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_316847334198b4fb.svg" alt="A_{\text{side}} = 4 \times 0.01" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m² <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9dc1f9db5add54ea.svg" alt="= 0.04" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m², anodised Al
> - Internal dissipation (peak mode, 10 W downlink — Table 8.4): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9c9e2297e033b907.svg" alt="Q_{\text{int}} = 10.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W. Essentially all electrical power drawn by the loads ends as heat inside the spacecraft; the RF power actually radiated by the antenna (a watt or two) is the only exception and is conservatively ignored here.
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bf68a68a7ccd883a.svg" alt="Q_{\text{solar}} = 0.85 \times 0.034 \times 1414 = 40.9" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W — but much of this is converted to electricity by the cells, so the net thermal input through the array is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a6c8dba2d49b835d.svg" alt="Q_{\text{solar,thermal}} = \alpha_s A S (1 - \eta_{\text{cell}}) = 0.85 \times 0.034 \times 1414 \times 0.705 = 28.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6d0a501379513a68.svg" alt="Q_{\text{albedo}} = 0.45 \times 0.034 \times 0.35 \times 1414 = 7.6" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_090c8223d1022759.svg" alt="Q_{\text{Earth IR}} = 0.82 \times 0.034 \times 270 = 7.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (nadir face, hot-case Earth IR)
>
> Total <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_60b088147b1463a6.svg" alt="Q_{\text{in}} \approx 28.8 + 7.6 + 7.5 + 10.0 = 53.9" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> Total radiating area (all six faces, less the array area, which is a net absorber, and allowing for partial Earth blockage of the nadir face): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f93c5a4a86dfbf62.svg" alt="A_{\text{rad}} \approx 0.066" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m²; average emissivity <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f72ca271c0feeca7.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{avg}} \approx 0.82" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3d3149149fcda352.svg" alt="T_{\text{hot}} = \left(\dfrac{53.9}{0.82 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.066}\right)^{1/4} = \left(\dfrac{53.9}{3.07 \times 10^{-9}}\right)^{1/4} = (1.756 \times 10^{10})^{1/4} = 364" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5e8937036bf6cfdd.svg" alt="= +91" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C
>
> **This exceeds most component limits!** However, this simplified calculation overestimates the temperature because it treats the satellite as a single isothermal node and lumps the solar-cell absorption on the zenith face into it. In practice:
>
> - The zenith face (solar cells) runs hotter than the bus
> - Internal components are conductively coupled to all faces, including the cold nadir face
> - A multi-node model typically predicts peak internal temperatures of +40 to +55 °C for this scenario
>
> **Thermal engineer's response:** If the single-node calculation exceeds 60 °C, a detailed multi-node thermal model is required. The simplified calculation is a screening tool, not a design tool.
>
> **Cold case (eclipse, safe mode, aphelion, BOL coatings):**
>
> - No solar flux, no albedo
> - Earth IR only: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bdebf94e787435c3.svg" alt="Q_{\text{Earth IR}} = 0.82 \times 0.034 \times 200 = 5.58" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (cold case: 200 W/m²)
> - Internal dissipation (safe mode, Table 8.4): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_da6d6750d62b85ad.svg" alt="Q_{\text{int}} = 2.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
> - Total <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a6503f4ae82f149b.svg" alt="Q_{\text{in}} = 5.58 + 2.0 = 7.58" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_54764d4b67bd9de3.svg" alt="T_{\text{cold}} = \left(\dfrac{7.58}{0.82 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.070}\right)^{1/4} = \left(\dfrac{7.58}{3.25 \times 10^{-9}}\right)^{1/4} = (2.33 \times 10^{9})^{1/4} = 220" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4325e82ef37a0735.svg" alt="= -53" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C
>
> **This is too cold** for Li-ion batteries (min −20 °C operating, min 0 °C charging) and most COTS electronics (min −40 °C) — *if* the spacecraft had time to reach steady state.
>
> **Steady-state heater check.** To hold the whole spacecraft at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_110b9aab97d5a2b2.svg" alt="T_{\text{min}} = -10" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_56cd62bbfa015dd7.svg" alt="= 263" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K would require
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b2dde77d9b30d74f.svg" alt="Q_{\text{heater}} = \varepsilon \sigma A_{\text{rad}} T_{\text{min}}^4 - Q_{\text{in}} = 3.25 \times 10^{-9} \times 263^4 - 7.58 = 15.6 - 7.58 = 8.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> An 8 W heater in eclipse would exceed the battery capacity. But this is an isothermal whole-spacecraft calculation: in reality the battery sits inside the bus, partially insulated by the structure and surrounding boards, and a targeted heater of 0.5–1.0 W on the battery pack, with some MLI wrapping, is typically sufficient. More importantly, the eclipse is only 36 minutes long and the structure's thermal mass prevents the satellite from approaching steady state at all.
>
> **Transient check.** In eclipse the net cooling rate is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1c3fe2e503e9f303.svg" alt="Q_{\text{out}} - Q_{\text{in}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. At eclipse entry, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b424341bb08daa6a.svg" alt="T = 293" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K (+20 °C):
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4c79c07913cadd03.svg" alt="Q_{\text{out}} = 0.82 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.070 \times 293^4 = 3.25 \times 10^{-9} \times 7.37 \times 10^{9} = 24.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e90bb91c5e318daa.svg" alt="Q_{\text{net cooling}} = 24.0 - 7.58 = 16.4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> For a 5 kg spacecraft with aluminium-dominated thermal mass (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_404265bfce13b924.svg" alt="c_p \approx 900" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> J/kg/K):
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fceaa7f2f0158002.svg" alt="\Delta T = \dfrac{Q_{\text{net}} \times t}{m \times c_p} = \dfrac{16.4 \times 2150}{5.0 \times 900} = \dfrac{35\,260}{4500} = 7.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C drop in 36 minutes
>
> So from +20 °C, the satellite cools to about +12 °C after one eclipse — well within limits (and the linear estimate is itself conservative, since <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bb46bed61d570479.svg" alt="Q_{\text{out}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> falls as <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_37ff4cb2f098cc8b.svg" alt="T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> as the spacecraft cools). **No heater needed for the bus; a battery heater only if the battery is thermally isolated from the bus.**
>
> **ECSS margin check — payload detector:**
> Predicted maximum temperature of the payload detector = 42 °C.
>
> - Operating limit = 50 °C. Margin = 50 − 42 = 8 °C > 5 °C. **Pass.**
> - Qualification test: must test at 42 + 15 = 57 °C. If the qualification limit is 60 °C: **Pass.**
>
> Predicted minimum temperature of the battery = −8 °C during the worst eclipse.
>
> - Operating limit = −10 °C. Margin = −8 − (−10) = 2 °C < 5 °C. **Fail — inadequate margin.**
> - **Action:** Add a 0.5 W survival heater with thermostat set to −5 °C, or add MLI around the battery pack.

---

## 9.5 Worked example: UniSat-1 power and thermal

Returning to UniSat-1, the 1U demonstrator of Chapter 1 §1.7, in the 400 km ISS orbit of Chapter 7 §7.7 (period 92.6 min, 56.5 min sunlight, 36 min eclipse).

**Power sizing: body-mounted only.** UniSat-1 uses body-mounted solar cells on all five Sun-exposed faces (the sixth face carries the deployment-switch interface). With no deployable panels, the power system is simpler, lighter and cheaper — but severely power-limited.

> **Worked example — UniSat-1 solar array**
>
> **Given:** Body-mounted cells on 5 faces of a 1U (100 × 100 mm each). <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4a5a89551f367fe2.svg" alt="P_{\text{ecl}} = 0.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (OBC only), <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_dcbdbc07505fd976.svg" alt="P_{\text{sun}} = 1.2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (science and downlink overlap avoided by scheduling). Mission lifetime 6 months. Cell temperature 55 °C (body-mounted cells run cooler on a 1U owing to good thermal coupling to the bus mass).
>
> **Step 1 — Effective illuminated area:**
> With passive magnetic attitude (slow tumble ~1°/s), on average only ~1.5 faces are well illuminated at any instant. Effective average area:
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_dc044d3fa929fecd.svg" alt="A_{\text{eff}} \approx 1.5 \times (0.10 \times 0.10) = 0.015" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m²
>
> **Step 2 — Array BOL power (with temperature derating):**
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8153380e93188889.svg" alt="L_T = 1 + (-0.0019)(55 - 28) = 0.949" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8076d60da35c3e0e.svg" alt="P_{\text{SA,BOL}} = \eta_{\text{cell}} \times L_T \times S \times A_{\text{eff}} \times f_{\text{pack}} = 0.295 \times 0.949 \times 1361 \times 0.015 \times 0.80 = 4.57" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (illuminated peak)
>
> **Step 3 — Orbit-average power available:**
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fb13dd8536622684.svg" alt="P_{\text{avg,avail}} = P_{\text{SA,BOL}} \times \dfrac{t_{\text{sun}}}{T} \times \eta_{\text{EPS}} = 4.57 \times \dfrac{56.5}{92.6} \times 0.85 = 2.37" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> After 6-month degradation (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d816f525fdc11b72.svg" alt="(1 - 0.025)^{0.5} = 0.987" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>): <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bc3c32f3aefb9006.svg" alt="P_{\text{avg,EOL}} = 2.37 \times 0.987 = 2.34" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> **Step 4 — Power demand (orbit average):** From Chapter 8 §8.5: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1a7d6ab04e8af7b6.svg" alt="P_{\text{avg,demand}} = 0.68" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W.
>
> **Power margin:** <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e9aff6c4a42469a3.svg" alt="2.34 - 0.68 = 1.66" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W (**71 % margin**). Even with conservative geometry assumptions, the budget closes comfortably.
>
> **Note on body-mounted arrays and tumbling:** The key uncertainty in 1U body-mounted power is the attitude. With passive magnetic stabilisation the satellite aligns roughly with Earth's magnetic field, providing more predictable illumination than a random tumble; however, the effective area varies significantly around the orbit as the field direction changes with latitude. The 1.5-face average is conservative — a Monte Carlo simulation of illumination geometry over many orbits typically yields a more optimistic 1.7–1.9 effective-face average.

> **Worked example — UniSat-1 battery**
>
> **Given:** <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4a5a89551f367fe2.svg" alt="P_{\text{ecl}} = 0.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_aa77bd934ee14180.svg" alt="t_{\text{ecl}} = 36" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3bbe8fa14593302a.svg" alt="= 0.60" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> h, DoD <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_64d5dbf225966cd0.svg" alt="= 0.50" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (acceptable for a 6-month mission: ~2 740 cycles), <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_520c0e396bc3a314.svg" alt="\eta_{\text{dis}} = 0.95" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d5ae07bfda2fbcaa.svg" alt="E_{\text{bat}} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 0.60}{0.50 \times 0.95} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.475} = 0.63" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> Wh
>
> With margin: specify minimum **10 Wh** — the smallest COTS CubeSat battery pack with flight heritage.
>
> **Cycle-count check:** 6 months at 15.5 orbits/day ≈ 2 800 eclipses. At 50 % DoD, Li-ion cells comfortably survive > 2 000 cycles. **Pass.**
>
> **Actual operating DoD:** With a 10 Wh battery and 0.63 Wh per eclipse, actual DoD = 0.63/10 = **6.3 %** per eclipse. At this DoD, cycle life exceeds 100 000 cycles. **Battery degradation is negligible** over the 6-month mission.
>
> **Key insight:** The 10 Wh battery is massively oversized for the actual eclipse demand. This is common in 1U missions — the minimum COTS battery available provides far more capacity than needed. The excess capacity provides excellent margin and enables recovery from anomalies (multiple missed sunlit periods).

**Thermal: passive only.** UniSat-1 uses no heaters, no MLI and no active thermal control. This is justified by three factors:

1. **Low altitude (400 km):** Strong Earth IR flux (~240 W/m²) provides a warm floor, preventing extreme cold cases
2. **Short mission (6 months):** No long-term coating degradation to worry about
3. **Tolerant components:** COTS electronics typically operate from −20 °C to +60 °C; the 400 km LEO thermal environment stays within −10 °C to +45 °C for a 1U with standard aluminium/anodised surfaces

> **Quick thermal check — UniSat-1 cold case (transient)**
>
> Worst eclipse, all subsystems off except OBC (0.5 W internal dissipation):
>
> - Earth IR absorbed: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_10788279865c18da.svg" alt="\varepsilon \times A_{\text{nadir}} \times q_{\text{IR}} = 0.85 \times 0.01 \times 240 = 2.04" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
> - Internal dissipation: 0.5 W
> - Total heat in: 2.54 W
>
> Steady-state temperature (if the eclipse were infinite):
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6df13a68f15c0386.svg" alt="T_{\text{steady}} = \left(2.54 / (0.85 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.045)\right)^{1/4} = 195" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7a75433507aee99a.svg" alt="= -78" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C
>
> **This looks alarming** — but the eclipse is only 36 minutes, and the thermal mass prevents the satellite from reaching steady state.
>
> **Transient analysis:** Starting at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cefebc8561dd3e49.svg" alt="T_0 = +20" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C (293 K) at eclipse entry:
>
> <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_331d0a873f1b3729.svg" alt="Q_{\text{rad,out}} = 0.85 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.045 \times 293^4 = 2.17 \times 10^{-9} \times 7.37 \times 10^{9} = 16.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> Net cooling: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e1829d1abe9fe5a0.svg" alt="16.0 - 2.54 = 13.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W
>
> Linear estimate: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6fdccde50d2d94a0.svg" alt="\Delta T = \dfrac{Q_{\text{net}} \times t}{m \times c_p} = \dfrac{13.5 \times 36 \times 60}{1.0 \times 900} = \dfrac{29\,160}{900} = 32" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C
>
> The linear estimate is conservative — as the satellite cools, the radiated power drops as <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_37ff4cb2f098cc8b.svg" alt="T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, so the actual cooling slows. A more accurate estimate gives <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_62df2c14924765ba.svg" alt="\Delta T \approx 20" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>–<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b8bc36041b1c39fe.svg" alt="25" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C, resulting in a minimum temperature of about −5 to −10 °C.
>
> **Conclusion:** The 1U at 400 km reaches approximately −5 to −10 °C during the worst-case eclipse, starting from a warm sunlit entry. This is within COTS operating limits (−20 °C to +60 °C for most components) and within the battery discharge range. **No heaters needed.** The short eclipse and the strong Earth IR flux at 400 km make passive thermal control viable for a 1U mission.

## 9.6 Real mission examples

### 9.6.1 Planet SuperDove EPS

| Parameter | Value | Design rationale |
|-----------|-------|-----------------|
| Form factor | 3U+, ~5 kg | Flock constellation; dispenser-compatible |
| SA configuration | Body-mounted + two deployable wings | ~25 W BOL needed for continuous imaging + S-band downlink |
| SA cells | Triple-junction GaAs | Standard space-grade, 29.5 % AM0 |
| Battery | Li-ion, ~20 Wh (2S2P 18650) | Supports ~3.5 W eclipse load for 35 min at < 20 % DoD |
| Bus voltage | Unregulated 7.2–8.4 V (2S) + regulated 3.3 V, 5 V | Standard CubeSat EPS architecture |
| Peak demand | ~18 W (imaging mode) | Multispectral imager + star tracker + reaction wheels + OBC |
| Orbit | 475 km SSO, ~94 min period | Sun-synchronous for consistent lighting |
| Eclipse | ~35 min max, ~3 W demand | OBC + AOCS only during eclipse; no imaging or downlink |
| Thermal | Body-mounted radiator panels + battery heater | Passive thermal control; battery heater for eclipse charging margin |

*[Source: Planet Labs conference presentations; Salas et al., "SuperDove Constellation," SSC 2021]*

### 9.6.2 CAPSTONE thermal design

NASA's CAPSTONE (12U, 25 kg) operates in a near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) around the Moon with extreme thermal cycling:

- Perilune: strong Earth/Moon IR + solar
- Apolune: deep-space cold, long shadow periods (up to 12+ hours)
- Thermal control: MLI wrapping (10-layer DAM blankets), heaters on propulsion lines (to prevent propellant freezing), passive radiator panels with white paint (AZ-93)
- Battery heaters: 5 W total, thermostatically controlled, critical for survival during long eclipses
- Operating temperature range: −20 °C to +50 °C for electronics; propulsion lines maintained above +5 °C

*[Source: Advanced Space, "CAPSTONE Design Overview," SmallSat Conference 2022]*

## Summary

| Topic | Key takeaway |
|-------|-------------|
| Solar cell physics | Triple-junction GaAs (InGaP/GaAs/Ge) achieves 28–30 % AM0; multi-junction stacking captures a broader solar spectrum |
| Temperature effects | Cells lose ~0.19 %/°C (relative); operating at 65 °C costs ~7 % power vs STC |
| Degradation | Radiation damage: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_78e35ee02c674d7f.svg" alt="(1-\delta)^n" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d4a540a07ac3fcb5.svg" alt="\delta \approx 2.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> %/yr LEO; cover glass mitigates proton/electron damage |
| EPS architecture | MPPT + regulated bus is the CubeSat standard; MPPT extracts 10–15 % more power than DET |
| SA sizing | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_03e7602d4e1f8b56.svg" alt="P_{\text{SA,EOL}} = (P_{\text{sun}} t_{\text{sun}}/\eta_{\text{sun}} + P_{\text{ecl}} t_{\text{ecl}}/\eta_{\text{ecl}})/t_{\text{sun}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; derate for degradation <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_baa14c9dfe0a37fd.svg" alt="L_d" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and temperature <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_20b2f3167b5bedde.svg" alt="L_T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> |
| SA area | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a4ee1c9c5dd8d3e0.svg" alt="A = P_{\text{BOL}} / (\eta_{\text{cell}} \cdot S \cdot \cos\theta \cdot f_{\text{pack}} \cdot f_{\text{cover}})" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; θ from the array geometry and the orbit β-angle |
| Battery chemistry | Li-ion (LCO/NMC): 150–200 Wh/kg packaged; 3.0–4.2 V per cell; CC–CV charging |
| Battery sizing | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3dfdd96fd03b5dea.svg" alt="E = P_{\text{ecl}} \cdot t_{\text{ecl}} / (\text{DoD} \cdot \eta_{\text{dis}})" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; DoD 20–30 % for multi-year LEO |
| Battery failure modes | Thermal runaway (overcharge), lithium plating (cold charge), capacity imbalance (series cells) |
| SA power reference | Body-mounted: 2–12 W; single deployable: 4–30 W; dual deployable: 25–48 W |
| Thermal physics | No convection in vacuum; radiation (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4c1e82e6851d72fe.svg" alt="\varepsilon \sigma T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) is the only mechanism for heat rejection |
| Thermal balance | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4688212db62d7125.svg" alt="Q_{\text{in}} = Q_{\text{out}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; solve for <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_936a0c5e392555f8.svg" alt="T = (Q/\varepsilon\sigma A)^{1/4}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (single node); multi-node for real design |
| <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> ratio | Low ratio = cold surface (radiator); high ratio = warm surface (insulation) |
| MLI construction | VDA Kapton outer + 10–20 DAM layers + Dacron spacers; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bc60029f067c4143.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} = 0.01" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>–<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7d7ef6eb96ec1cc3.svg" alt="0.03" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> |
| Heater sizing | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5438c5a0e548325c.svg" alt="P_{\text{heater}} = \varepsilon\sigma A T_{\text{min}}^4 - Q_{\text{env}} - Q_{\text{int}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; Kapton foil heaters, thermostat control |
| Thermal margins | ECSS: ±5 °C operating, ±10 °C acceptance, ±15 °C qualification |
| Transient effects | Thermal mass (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2f32a32845c46939.svg" alt="mc_p" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) prevents reaching steady state during short eclipses; a 1U at 400 km cools ~20–25 °C in a 36-min eclipse |

## Problems

1. **Array sizing.** A 3U Earth-observation CubeSat in a 550 km Sun-synchronous orbit (compute <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5f8eb8cbe0662591.svg" alt="T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_08975aafdd68bf6f.svg" alt="t_{\text{sun}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f2d3d7241b2566a5.svg" alt="t_{\text{ecl}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at β = 0 using Chapter 7) has a peak sunlit demand of 12 W and an eclipse load of 4 W. Size the solar array for a 4-year mission with cells at 70 °C and an effective Sun angle of 25°, showing all five steps. What array area and mass result?

2. **Path efficiency sensitivity.** Repeat the EOSat-3U worked example of §9.2 with the lumped <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b41bd199f2a59d4f.svg" alt="\eta_{\text{ecl}} = 0.90" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> in place of 0.786, and with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7829a5c90758b203.svg" alt="\eta_{\text{sun}} = 1" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (no daytime regulator loss). By what percentage does the required BOL power change in each case? Which assumption would you accept at Phase A, and why?

3. **Sun angle and β.** For the EOSat-3U orbit (10:30 LTAN, assume β between 20° and 30° through the year), compare the orbit-averaged <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0940bd72bfb6133c.svg" alt="\cos\theta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> of (a) a side-mounted panel whose normal is perpendicular to the orbit plane and (b) the zenith face. Which mounting gives more energy per orbit, and how does the answer change for a dawn–dusk (β ≈ 85°) orbit?

4. **Battery sizing and cycle life.** Size the battery for the spacecraft of Problem 1 at 20 % and 35 % DoD. For each, compute the number of eclipse cycles over 4 years and check against the cycle-life table. Which DoD would you choose, and what battery mass does it imply at 170 Wh/kg?

5. **Orbit-average closure.** Using the mode table of Chapter 8 Table 8.4 and the duty cycles of §8.4.4, confirm the orbit-average demand of 4.63 W. Then compute the orbit-average power the array of §9.2 actually delivers (BOL power × sunlit fraction × <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_768e55917b9c3c0c.svg" alt="\eta_{\text{sun}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) and show whether the orbit-energy balance closes at BOL and at EOL.

6. **Hot-case screening.** Repeat the single-node hot-case calculation of §9.4.11 for a spacecraft whose zenith face is white-painted structure (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a3f64d80dc00fd1a.svg" alt="\alpha_s = 0.30" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> EOL, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d79a33c719580e65.svg" alt="\varepsilon = 0.90" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) instead of solar cells, with the array moved to a deployable wing that is thermally decoupled from the bus. What single-node temperature results, and what does the comparison tell you about where the array should be mounted from a thermal point of view?

7. **Transient cooling.** Integrate the eclipse cool-down of §9.4.11 numerically (time steps of 2 minutes, recomputing <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bb46bed61d570479.svg" alt="Q_{\text{out}}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at each step) and compare the result with the 7.8 °C linear estimate. Then repeat for the 1U UniSat-1 case and compare with the 20–25 °C quoted in §9.5.

8. **Heater sizing.** A battery pack of 0.15 kg (effective <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_550ee47f9156bf50.svg" alt="c_p = 1000" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> J/kg/K) is wrapped in MLI with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_da4fcf63f1295327.svg" alt="\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} = 0.03" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and radiating area 0.01 m², and enters eclipse at +15 °C. Estimate its cool-down over 36 minutes with no heater, and size a thermostat-controlled heater that holds it above 0 °C. What fraction of the eclipse energy budget of §9.3 does the heater consume?

9. **ECSS margins.** The predicted temperature range for a star tracker is −18 °C to +48 °C and its operating limits are −30 °C to +60 °C. Check the operating margin, state the acceptance and qualification test temperatures, and decide whether the design passes. If the qualification limit of the unit is +60 °C, what must change?

10. **UniSat-1 trade.** Suppose UniSat-1 adds a single deployable 1U panel (0.01 m², <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6880829b318d5078.svg" alt="\theta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> ≈ 30° average). Recompute the orbit-average power available and the margin. Then list the three new interfaces (Chapter 8 §8.3) and the one new failure mode the panel introduces, and argue whether the extra 1 W is worth it for a magnetometer mission.
