## Cost Engineer

You are the team's reality check.

### Decisions you own

1. **WBS structure** (Chapter 16 §16.2, after NPR 7120.5).
2. **Cost-estimating method** — parametric early, analogy, bottom-up later (Chapter 16 §16.1).
3. **Schedule baseline** — milestones, critical path, float (with the Project Manager).
4. **Risk-adjusted estimates** — how to roll risk into both cost and schedule (Chapter 16 §16.4).

### What you need to know first

- **The bill of materials** from Chapter 13 — equipment costs, lead times and TRL (§13.2 for the TRL risk factor).
- **Non-recurring engineering** — Chapter 13 §13.1.3 gives the NRE build-up; do not restate it in the parametric model.
- **The number of units** — the learning curve of Chapter 16 §16.3 (with the exponent of Chapter 4 §4.6.4) changes the answer for a constellation.
- **The programmatic ceiling** and what the sponsor counts as "cost" (launch, operations, ground segment in or out).

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **Cost-estimating relationships** and their accuracy by phase — Chapter 16 §16.1.
- **Learning curve** — Chapter 16 §16.3: on a 90 % curve the tenth unit costs 70 % of the first, and twenty units cost 14.6 times the first, not twenty.
- **Cost risk** — the P50/P80 S-curve of Chapter 16 §16.4; report P80, manage to P50.
- **Worked numbers** — the EOSat-3U estimate in Chapter 16 §16.1 and the UniSat-1 roll-up (about 85 kEUR, indicative 2026) in Chapter 13 §13.6 and Chapter 16 §16.4.3.

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake.** Treating the parametric tool's output as the answer. The output is a starting point; tailor it for your mission and the launch market you are working in.

> **Watch out.** CubeSat COTS prices date fast and are quoted without integration, test or spares. Mark every price with its year and what it includes.

### References

- NASA NPR 7120.5F — [https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/](https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/).
- Wertz et al., *Space Mission Engineering*, Ch. 23 (cost).
- SMAD4 Ch. 20.
- NASA *Cost Estimating Handbook* — [https://www.nasa.gov/cost-estimating-handbook/](https://www.nasa.gov/cost-estimating-handbook/).

---

## Compliance Engineer

You make sure the mission is allowed to fly — by the standards it has adopted, by the regulators who license it, and by the export-control regimes its parts came through.

### Decisions you own

1. **Standards applicability and tailoring.** Which ECSS / NASA standards apply and at what level — the tailoring matrix (Chapter 3 §3.2, after ECSS-S-ST-00-02C).
2. **Frequency licensing strategy.** Amateur (IARU) vs commercial allocation; the ITU advance publication, the national filing and their lead times (Chapter 2 §2.7).
3. **Export-control classification** for every component (ITAR / EAR / Canadian controlled goods), with Procurement (Chapter 2 §2.8, Chapter 13 §13.4).
4. **Debris-mitigation compliance** — 25-year IADC, 5-year FCC where it applies, casualty risk (Chapter 3 §3.6, Chapter 7 §7.3.2).
5. **Remote-sensing licence** under the RSSSA if the mission images the Earth (Chapter 2 §2.6), and registration of the object after launch (Chapter 3 §3.7).

### What you need to know first

- **The orbit and lifetime** from the Mission Analyst — the debris case stands or falls on it.
- **The band, EIRP and ground stations** from Communications — the filing cannot start without them.
- **The bill of materials** from Chapter 13 — origin and classification of every part.
- **Payload resolution and data-distribution plan** from the Payload Lead and User Representative — these decide whether the RSSSA applies and at what level.

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **The compliance register** — the format of Chapter 3 Table 3.1: standard or regulation, the parameter it depends on, the phase by which it must be closed, the evidence.
- **Licensing timeline** — the lead times of Chapter 2 §2.7.4; spectrum coordination is routinely the longest pole in a CubeSat schedule, and it starts before the design is frozen.
- **Rule of thumb.** Every regulatory filing is a requirement with a verification method (Chapter 14): put it in the verification matrix with a date, not in a memo.

### Common pitfalls

> **Watch out.** Starting the frequency filing after the design is frozen. Coordination takes a year or more; a band change late in Phase B rewrites the link budget, the antenna and the licence.

> **Common mistake.** Assuming a COTS part is export-free because it was bought from a catalogue. Classification follows the part's origin and its technology, not its price.

> **Watch out.** Debris compliance is assessed on the spacecraft as flown — the deployed area, the final mass, the actual altitude — not on the Phase A numbers. Re-run it at every gate.

### References

- ECSS-S-ST-00-02C — Tailoring — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- ISED, *Client Procedures Circular CPC-2-6-02* (licensing of space stations) — [https://ised-isde.canada.ca/](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/).
- *Remote Sensing Space Systems Act* (RSSSA) and regulations — [https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/).
- ITU Radio Regulations, Article 9 (coordination) — [https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR](https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR).
- IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines — [https://www.iadc-home.org/](https://www.iadc-home.org/).

---

## User Representative

You speak for the people who will use the data. The mission is a success when they say it is, not when the budgets close.

### Decisions you own

1. **Data product requirements** — format, resolution, accuracy, timeliness (with the Payload Lead: Chapter 4 §4.3).
2. **User access methods** — API, portal, direct download (with Ground Segment: Chapter 17 §17.1).
3. **Service levels** — availability, response time, data freshness.
4. **Validation** that the system as designed meets what the stakeholders asked for (Chapter 14 §14.1 — validation is your word, verification is the engineers').
5. **The user's voice in trade studies** — you sit on the trade-study panel of Chapter 4 §4.5 and score the options from the user's side.

### What you need to know first

- **Who the users are** — research, commercial, public, operational — and how they differ (Chapter 4 §4.2).
- **What they do with the data today**, without this mission, so that you can state the need rather than the wish.
- **The downlink and latency the system can actually deliver** (Chapter 11 §11.9, Chapter 17 §17.2), so that the service level you promise is one the mission can keep.

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **Need → objective → MoE → MoP → TPM** — the hierarchy of Chapter 4 §4.3.3 is your instrument; every data-product requirement should trace up to a measure of effectiveness the user recognises.
- **The WHAT-not-HOW test** of Chapter 4 §4.1.4: if your requirement names an implementation, rewrite it.
- **Rule of thumb.** A "nice to have" that cannot be traded away is a requirement; a requirement that nobody would miss is a nice-to-have. Sort them before the first trade study, not during it.

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake.** Not distinguishing between "nice to have" and actual requirements — and letting the engineers guess which is which.

> **Watch out.** Specifying implementation details (a band, a file format, a satellite) instead of user needs (a latency, a coverage, an accuracy).

> **Watch out.** Assuming unlimited bandwidth for data delivery. The daily volume the spacecraft can downlink (Figure 11.6) is the ceiling on what any user can receive, however good the portal.

### References

- NASA SEH §4.1 — Stakeholder expectations definition — [https://www.nasa.gov/reference/systems-engineering-handbook/](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/systems-engineering-handbook/).
- ECSS-E-ST-10C §5.2 — Requirements engineering — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- ISO 9241 — Ergonomics of human-system interaction.

---

## Mission Operations Engineer

You will fly the spacecraft after the team builds it — and you rehearse doing so before launch (Chapter 19).

### Decisions you own

1. **Operations concept** — staffing, automation level, shift structure (Chapter 18 §18.1).
2. **Pass plan** — which procedures, in what order, every contact (Chapter 18 §18.4, Chapter 17 §17.4).
3. **Anomaly response tree** — who calls what, when (Chapter 18 §18.5).
4. **Telecommand and telemetry definition** — coordination with the Software Engineer.
5. **LEOP sequence** — first contact, deployments, commissioning timeline (Chapter 19 §19.4).

### What you need to know first

- **The operational modes and their transitions** from the ConOps (Chapter 18 §18.2 and Table 18.1).
- **Ground-station coverage** from the Mission Analyst and Ground Segment (Chapter 17 §17.2).
- **The FDIR architecture** — what the spacecraft will do on its own before you hear about it (Chapter 18 §18.3).
- **The procedure inventory** — LEOP, commissioning, nominal, contingency, emergency.

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **Contact time per day and data per pass** — Chapter 17 §17.2.3; a high-latitude station sees a SSO spacecraft on most orbits, a mid-latitude one on four to six.
- **The anomaly library** — Chapter 19 §19.5 lists the symptoms, diagnoses and recoveries worth rehearsing (under-voltage, loss of contact, loss of fine pointing, unexpected safe mode, thermal exceedance, mass memory full, command rejected, and the ground fault that looks like a spacecraft fault).
- **Rule of thumb.** The first eight hours after separation are the most critical of the mission; script them to the minute, and rehearse the script.

### Common pitfalls

> **Watch out.** Voice-loop discipline is the silent killer. Cross-talk that sounds harmless in rehearsal breaks down under real-time pressure.

> **Common mistake.** Not planning for degraded operations — a single ground station, a partial deployment, office-hours staffing when the plan assumed 24/7.

> **Watch out.** Seasonal and geometric gaps in station visibility; a station that is fine in the simulation may be unusable at the β-angles of launch season.

### References

- ECSS-E-ST-70C — Ground systems and operations — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- ECSS-E-ST-70-32C — Test and operations procedure language.
- NASA-HDBK-1002 — Fault management handbook; GSFC-STD-1000 — Rules for the design, development, verification and operation of flight systems.

---

## Ground Segment Engineer

You own the architecture between the antenna and the user.

### Decisions you own

1. **Ground-station network** — owned, leased or commercial; a single station or a network (Chapter 17 §17.1, §17.5).
2. **Mission-control software** — open-source or commercial.
3. **Archive and processing design** — L0 → L1 → L2 → distribution, and the latency of each step.
4. **Pass-planning and scheduling tools.**
5. **Cyber-security architecture** — command authentication, link encryption, network segregation.

### What you need to know first

- **Daily data volume** — drives bandwidth contracts and archive growth.
- **Latency requirement** from the User Representative — drives station density.
- **Mission classification** — defence and dual-use missions need different architectures from civil ones.
- **The protocol stack** the spacecraft will speak (Chapter 17 §17.3).

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **Contact geometry** — Chapter 7 §7.4.1 and Chapter 17 §17.2: the pass profile of Figure 17.2, the maximum pass of 7.4 min at 500 km with a 10° mask, 9.2 min at 5°.
- **Daily capacity** — the station-by-station volumes of Chapter 17 §17.2.3 and the closure against generation in §17.5; the UniSat-1 shortfall with one station is worked in §17.6.
- **Rule of thumb.** Commercial ground-station pricing can flip the economics between bands and between a few long passes and many short ones; do the arithmetic at the data rate you will actually fly.

### Common pitfalls

> **Watch out.** Pricing models for ground-station-as-a-service charge by the minute or by the pass; the cheapest band on paper may not be the cheapest per megabyte.

> **Common mistake.** Designing the ground segment after the space segment is frozen. The station network is part of the link budget (Chapter 11 §11.7) and part of the data budget (§11.9); it belongs in the first design loop.

### References

- CCSDS Mission Operations and cross-support standards — [https://public.ccsds.org/Pubs/](https://public.ccsds.org/Pubs/).
- ECSS-E-ST-70C — Ground systems and operations — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- SMAD4 Ch. 14–15.

---

## Software Engineer (OBDH and flight software)

You own the flight computer, the flight software, the telemetry list and the on-board half of FDIR.

### Decisions you own

1. **OBC architecture** — single board or redundant pair; system-on-chip vs discrete (Chapter 12 §12.3).
2. **Bus topology** — CAN / I²C / SPI / RS-422 / SpaceWire (the interface types of Chapter 8 Table 8.2).
3. **Memory architecture** — RAM, flash, mass memory, EDAC scheme (Chapter 12 §12.3.3 for sizing).
4. **Flight-software architecture** — mode manager, AOCS control loop, TM/TC handler, FDIR rules (Chapter 18 §18.3).
5. **Service set** — which CCSDS/PUS services to implement; the telecommand and telemetry dictionaries.

### What you need to know first

- **TM/TC volume** from each subsystem.
- **Real-time loop rates** required by AOCS.
- **The longest no-contact gap** — sizes the mass memory (Chapter 12 §12.3.3; EOSat-3U uses a three-day outage case).
- **The ground software** it must talk to (Chapter 17 §17.3).

### Formulas, charts, rules of thumb

- **Mass-memory sizing** — longest contact gap × peak data rate × a margin of 1.5–2; Chapter 12 §12.3.3 works the EOSat-3U case.
- **Watchdog timer** — typically 30 s for a CubeSat OBC; shorter for high-criticality threads. Chapter 15 §15.5 carries the OBC watchdog as risk R-03 for UniSat-1.
- **EDAC overhead** — Hamming SECDED costs about 12.5 % for 64-bit words.
- **Rule of thumb.** The I²C-versus-RS-422 interface example of Chapter 8 §8.3 is the shape of most OBDH interface conflicts: the bus is chosen for convenience and discovered to be wrong for noise or distance at integration.

### Common pitfalls

> **Watch out.** Telemetry-list overruns are the number-one late OBDH defect. Lock the list at SRR; treat any addition as a change-control item.

> **Common mistake.** Writing FDIR rules that are not testable on the ground. Every rule in Chapter 18 §18.3 should have a test case in the verification matrix (Chapter 14 §14.4).

### References

- ECSS-E-ST-70-41C — Telemetry and telecommand packet utilisation (PUS) — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- ECSS-E-ST-40C — Software; ECSS-Q-ST-80C — Software product assurance — [https://ecss.nl/](https://ecss.nl/).
- CCSDS 133.0-B — Space Packet Protocol — [https://public.ccsds.org/Pubs/](https://public.ccsds.org/Pubs/).


# Part V — First-Principles Derivations

This part derives, from first principles, the formulas applied in Parts I–III. Every derivation is paired with a worked sanity check against a published reference value, and — where the chapters do not already show it — with a plot of the formula in action.

The aim is twofold: (a) to give the reader a place to look up the *why* behind any formula they are applying; (b) to provide a worked verification trail that a reviewer can audit at a design review. Where the same equation appears in a chapter of Parts I–III, the derivation here uses exactly the symbols of that chapter, so that the two can be read side by side.

> **Standard reference.** The constants and conventions used throughout this part follow Vallado, *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications* (4th ed.) and the IERS Conventions 2010 — [https://www.iers.org/IERS/EN/Publications/TechnicalNotes/tn36.html](https://www.iers.org/IERS/EN/Publications/TechnicalNotes/tn36.html).

---

|--------|-------|---------|--------|
| <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b990e4f8ae9f3348.svg" alt="\mu" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | 398 600.44 km³/s² | Earth gravitational parameter | IERS Conventions 2010 |
| <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d8530cb5957a7f4c.svg" alt="R_E" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | 6378.137 km | Earth equatorial radius | WGS-84 |

These are the values used in every worked number in Parts I–III. ## V.2 — Kepler's Third Law

### Derivation

For a circular orbit of radius <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0fbdd907aba23d4d.svg" alt="a" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, centripetal acceleration equals gravitational attraction:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_65596ded67dfde7e.svg" alt="\frac{v^2}{a} = \frac{\mu}{a^2}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Substitute <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7ead126ac59f432f.svg" alt="v = 2\pi a / T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and solve for <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5f8eb8cbe0662591.svg" alt="T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_56bf27b77e156a61.svg" alt="T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{\mu}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



For elliptical orbits the same formula applies with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0fbdd907aba23d4d.svg" alt="a" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> the semi-major axis. The circular velocity is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cf60e0864ee2ce67.svg" alt="v = \sqrt{\mu/a}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. These are the forms used in Chapter 7 §7.1.1.

### Verification

Figure D.1 overplots the analytical curve with the periods of known orbits.

![Kepler's Third Law verified against known orbits.](../assets/figures/fig_kepler_proof.png)

**Figure D.1** — The analytical period–altitude curve overplotted with known orbits (ISS, Sentinel-2, GPS, GEO). Agreement is to better than 0.5 %, the remaining error attributable to the <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9b3c6c687ea02746.svg" alt="J_2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> secular correction not applied here. At GEO, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2c158d749cef06af.svg" alt="T = 1436" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min against the sidereal day of 23.93 h × 60 = 1436 min.

**Worked sanity check.** For a 450 km Sun-synchronous orbit:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1507b1995e490953.svg" alt="a = 6378.137 + 450 = 6828.137" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3365b688c5860785.svg" alt="a^3/\mu = 6828.137^3 / 398\,600.44 = 7.987 \times 10^5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> s²; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_38ff2d33b08b45b5.svg" alt="\sqrt{\,\cdot\,} = 893.7" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> s;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_58bca191c0a44b39.svg" alt="T = 2\pi \times 893.7 = 5615" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> s <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_848a7059495c25b7.svg" alt="= 93.6" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min.

The same arithmetic at 500 km gives <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e8dba438f51c5065.svg" alt="a = 6878.137" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d6dc9f41bc66f02e.svg" alt="T = 94.6" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min, and at 400 km gives 92.6 min — the values used throughout Chapter 7 and the subsystem chapters. Expressed as a mean motion, 93.6 min is 15.38 revolutions per day; the slightly lower figures quoted in two-line element sets for real spacecraft at this altitude (≈ 15.2–15.3 rev/day) reflect the <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9b3c6c687ea02746.svg" alt="J_2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> perturbation of the nodal period, not an error in the formula.

---

## V.3 — Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation

### Derivation

For a rocket with constant exhaust velocity <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9a3fde70ec84cf74.svg" alt="v_e" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, momentum conservation between time <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_46078b62a6ebd9dc.svg" alt="t" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_91f3dac752528a6d.svg" alt="t + dt" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> gives



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8430024ddd176a51.svg" alt="m\, dv = -v_e\, dm" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Integrate from <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c4d9775fedeaa4b9.svg" alt="m_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (initial total mass) to <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_50e4cc2e7d28c075.svg" alt="m_f" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (final dry mass):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4c0e54016c51f865.svg" alt="\Delta V = v_e \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f} = I_{sp}\, g_0\, \ln \frac{m_0}{m_f}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



since <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a1ca6913dc2e174c.svg" alt="v_e = I_{sp}\, g_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> by the definition of specific impulse. The propellant mass follows as <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cdbbc96f7bf6a5ac.svg" alt="m_p = m_f\,(e^{\Delta V/(I_{sp} g_0)} - 1)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the total impulse as <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c425e414ecf1e94e.svg" alt="I_{tot} = m_p\, I_{sp}\, g_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. Chapter 12 §12.2.2 applies the equation and Figure 12.2 plots <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9c46368dea9fdb04.svg" alt="\Delta V" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> against mass ratio for representative specific impulses.

### Verification

**Worked sanity check.** Hohmann transfer from a 400 km circular orbit to GEO (the case plotted in Chapter 7 Figure 7.4):

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7c635c802ac1e7a6.svg" alt="r_1 = 6778.137" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_33c56ef64a3efc51.svg" alt="r_2 = 42\,164" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cc45333f0cbe1d99.svg" alt="a_t = (r_1 + r_2)/2 = 24\,471" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km.

At perigee: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bbb899268cc60d6a.svg" alt="v_1 = \sqrt{\mu/r_1} = 7.669" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1523fd23820a8f48.svg" alt="v_p = \sqrt{\mu\,(2/r_1 - 1/a_t)} = 10.061" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_46703cee424dce51.svg" alt="\Delta V_1 = 2.392" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s.

At apogee: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_deecfe17f75c9407.svg" alt="v_2 = \sqrt{\mu/r_2} = 3.075" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_58958bd73285b773.svg" alt="v_a = \sqrt{\mu\,(2/r_2 - 1/a_t)} = 1.610" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b7a3fb947c88e8d1.svg" alt="\Delta V_2 = 1.465" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s.

Total <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ac14e55948f60951.svg" alt="\Delta V = 3.857" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s — matching Figure 7.4 (3.854 km/s) to within rounding. For the deorbit case of Chapter 12 §12.2.5 (600 km circular to a 200 km perigee) the same vis-viva arithmetic gives 112 m/s.

---

## V.4 — <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9b3c6c687ea02746.svg" alt="J_2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> Nodal Regression

### Derivation

The dominant secular perturbation from Earth's oblateness <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9b3c6c687ea02746.svg" alt="J_2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> produces a nodal regression rate (Vallado eq. 9-37):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c300679deeb2ed85.svg" alt="\dot{\Omega} = -\frac{3}{2}\, n\, J_2\, \left(\frac{R_E}{a(1-e^2)}\right)^2 \cos i" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2e75575d01e5645f.svg" alt="n = \sqrt{\mu/a^3}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the mean motion. The minus sign means the node regresses for prograde orbits (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_89062be58f24572f.svg" alt="\cos i &gt; 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) and progresses for retrograde orbits (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ca921f69e60221ba.svg" alt="\cos i &lt; 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>).

### Sun-synchronous condition

For a Sun-synchronous orbit, set <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fee7bdc0473f352e.svg" alt="\dot{\Omega}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> equal to Earth's mean motion around the Sun (360°/365.25 days = 0.9856°/day = 1.991 × 10⁻⁷ rad/s):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5571027a7cb75ea5.svg" alt="\cos i_{SSO} = -\frac{2\, \dot{\Omega}_\odot\, a^{7/2}\, (1-e^2)^2}{3\, J_2\, R_E^2\, \sqrt{\mu}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



This is the condition applied in Chapter 7 §7.3.4.

### Verification

Figure D.2 shows the regression rate against inclination for several altitudes.

![J₂ nodal regression rate versus inclination at several altitudes.](../assets/figures/fig_j2_nodal.png)

**Figure D.2** — Nodal regression rate <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fee7bdc0473f352e.svg" alt="\dot{\Omega}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> as a function of inclination for several altitudes. The dashed horizontal at 0.9856°/day is the Sun-synchronous target; its intersection with each altitude curve gives the Sun-synchronous inclination at that altitude (≈ 98.2° at 700 km).

**Worked sanity check.** For 700 km circular (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bcd3b1ba89ad642a.svg" alt="e = 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>):

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ef6a759ff09071f6.svg" alt="a = 7078.137" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d25c9a3747081c21.svg" alt="n = \sqrt{398\,600.44 / 7078.137^3} = 1.060 \times 10^{-3}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> rad/s;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d032333ec8740c1a.svg" alt="\dot{\Omega}_\odot = 2\pi/(365.25 \times 86\,400) = 1.991 \times 10^{-7}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> rad/s;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9c513c0cf639f41e.svg" alt="\cos i = -(2 \times 1.991 \times 10^{-7} \times 7078.137^{7/2}) / (3 \times 1.0826 \times 10^{-3} \times 6378.137^2 \times \sqrt{398\,600.44}) = -0.143" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7eef00ded94b293e.svg" alt="i = \arccos(-0.143) = 98.2°" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.

At 600 km the same calculation gives 97.8°, and at 500 km 97.4° — the Chapter 7 values.

## V.5 — Eclipse Fraction (analytical, circular orbit)

### Derivation

For a circular orbit of altitude <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, the spacecraft is in eclipse when the line to the Sun is occulted by the Earth (the cylindrical-shadow approximation, which neglects the penumbra). Let <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d231046189335742.svg" alt="\beta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> be the angle between the Sun vector and the orbit plane. Seen from the orbit, the Earth subtends a half-angle <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b2329fd5415d1619.svg" alt="\beta^* = \arcsin\!\big(R_E/(R_E+h)\big)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; for <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_90b7a7402f93d24f.svg" alt="|\beta| \ge \beta^*" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> the orbit never crosses the shadow.

For <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8b567b16ca2ab853.svg" alt="|\beta| &lt; \beta^*" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, project the geometry onto the orbit plane. The shadow cylinder of radius <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d8530cb5957a7f4c.svg" alt="R_E" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> cuts the orbit plane in an ellipse whose semi-minor axis (across the Sun line) is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d8530cb5957a7f4c.svg" alt="R_E" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and whose semi-major axis (along the Sun line) is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2ad0b8bc8b413051.svg" alt="R_E/\cos\beta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The spacecraft, at radius <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_02b27443204de24f.svg" alt="R_E + h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, is in shadow over the arc of orbit angle <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d6ec234d6bfa1ae1.svg" alt="2\phi" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> for which its across-Sun-line distance is less than <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d8530cb5957a7f4c.svg" alt="R_E" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and its along-Sun-line position is on the anti-Sun side; solving the ellipse intersection gives



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7314881bdac5253e.svg" alt="\cos\phi = \frac{\sqrt{h^2 + 2 R_E h}}{(R_E + h)\cos\beta}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



and hence the eclipse fraction of the orbit period (Wertz, *Mission Geometry*, eq. 5-24):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6620a4530c13a75a.svg" alt="f_{ecl} = \frac{1}{\pi}\, \arccos\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{h^2 + 2 R_E h}}{(R_E + h) \cos\beta}\right), \qquad |\beta| &lt; \beta^*" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fd560d53c0fb1228.svg" alt="f_{ecl} = 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> for <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_90b7a7402f93d24f.svg" alt="|\beta| \ge \beta^*" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. This is the form given in Chapter 7 §7.1.2.

**Corollary (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_735cac4947ee2211.svg" alt="\beta = 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>).** With the Sun in the orbit plane the argument becomes <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e2c0a5652663daf8.svg" alt="\sqrt{h^2 + 2R_E h}/(R_E+h) = \cos\beta^*" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, so



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_73128c0c1a1fc058.svg" alt="f_{ecl,max} = \frac{\beta^*}{\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



— the maximum-eclipse case used for power and thermal sizing (Chapter 7 presents this as the corollary; Chapter 9 §9.2–§9.3 use it). The eclipse duration is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8a51dcbb5ce21632.svg" alt="t_{ecl} = f_{ecl}\,T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.

### Verification

The annual <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d231046189335742.svg" alt="\beta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> envelope and the eclipse-fraction curves for an ISS-like orbit and a 600 km Sun-synchronous orbit are plotted in Chapter 7 Figure 7.2: both show the characteristic plateau at low <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_bf2818bf8148aafb.svg" alt="|\beta|" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the sharp transition at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d0f06ce5700c2742.svg" alt="\beta^*" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.

**Worked sanity check.** ISS-like orbit, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6d52c142c138ea60.svg" alt="h = 400" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_735cac4947ee2211.svg" alt="\beta = 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e12334d6f8175c51.svg" alt="\beta^* = \arcsin(6378.137 / 6778.137) = \arcsin(0.9410) = 70.2°" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f26c02ee02dc683d.svg" alt="h^2 + 2 R_E h = 160\,000 + 5\,102\,510 = 5\,262\,510" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km²; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7033fe7cc2f0ea39.svg" alt="\sqrt{\,\cdot\,} = 2294.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km;
argument <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d37460046f10a585.svg" alt="= 2294.0 / 6778.137 = 0.3384" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d2c331ae1e32cc1f.svg" alt="\arccos(0.3384) = 70.2° = 1.2256" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> rad;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6d0eb7250e4a1f62.svg" alt="f_{ecl} = 1.2256/\pi = 0.390 \approx 39\,\%" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.

This agrees with the corollary (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_67581d80fa3bfaf1.svg" alt="\beta^*/\pi = 70.2°/180° = 0.390" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) and with the observed ISS maximum eclipse fraction of about 39 % (≈ 36 min of a 92.6 min orbit). At 500 km the same calculation gives <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_70ce895fee9bcbec.svg" alt="f_{ecl,max} = 0.378" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d179dd25f4c89ff5.svg" alt="t_{ecl} = 35.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min — the EOSat-3U values of Chapter 7 §7.2 and Chapter 9.

---

## V.6 — Free-Space Path Loss

### Derivation

An isotropic radiator of power <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_55ecee35bb0850e3.svg" alt="P_t" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at distance <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_945065a16f802f44.svg" alt="d" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> produces a power flux <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_57437df037bfacde.svg" alt="P_t / (4\pi d^2)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. A receiving antenna of effective aperture <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5a460559e0bba692.svg" alt="A_e" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> captures <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5a460559e0bba692.svg" alt="A_e" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> times the flux, and antenna theory relates aperture to gain by <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e563085eb537ea07.svg" alt="A_e = G_r \lambda^2 / (4\pi)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. With a directional transmit antenna of gain <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a8a4b0cecf15f8ae.svg" alt="G_t" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> the received power is the Friis transmission equation:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_01b723edaea05c4a.svg" alt="P_r = P_t\, G_t\, G_r \left(\frac{\lambda}{4 \pi d}\right)^2" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



The free-space path loss is the inverse of the geometric term, in decibels:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_facd056fa2bcde8f.svg" alt="\text{FSPL} = 20 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4 \pi d}{\lambda}\right) = 20 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4 \pi d f}{c}\right)\ \text{dB}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



No energy is absorbed: the <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8427a65248c4e1cb.svg" alt="d^2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> term is spherical spreading and the <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_497a9a95feac9625.svg" alt="\lambda^2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> term is the shrinking capture area of a fixed-gain antenna at higher frequency. Each doubling of <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_945065a16f802f44.svg" alt="d" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> or of <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_564eb7b8172b11af.svg" alt="f" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> adds 6.02 dB. Chapter 11 §11.4 and Figure 11.3 plot the loss by band against slant range.

### Verification

**Worked sanity check.** S-band (2.2 GHz) at 1500 km slant range:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a9c80b4dbf692bde.svg" alt="\lambda = c/f = 2.998 \times 10^8 / 2.2 \times 10^9 = 0.1363" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cf2a678c282036b1.svg" alt="\text{FSPL} = 20\log_{10}(4\pi \times 1.5 \times 10^6 / 0.1363) = 20\log_{10}(1.383 \times 10^8) = 162.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> dB.

For the EOSat-3U worked case of Chapter 11 §11.8 (2.25 GHz, 1695 km slant range at 10° elevation) the same formula gives 164.1 dB, which is the FSPL bar of the link-budget waterfall in Chapter 11 Figure 11.5.

---

## V.7 — Link-Budget Algebra

### Derivation

Write the Friis equation of V.6 in decibels and collect the transmitter terms into the effective isotropic radiated power, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_aec74ccb0e4dc0c0.svg" alt="\text{EIRP} = P_{TX} + G_{TX} - L_{TX}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (dBW). Adding the losses that free space does not include — atmospheric absorption <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d2be35e36cde337c.svg" alt="L_{atm}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, antenna mispointing <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7e14be0389ac9ac4.svg" alt="L_{point}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, polarisation mismatch <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_af9806028adba40d.svg" alt="L_{pol}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the receive-side feed and line loss <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f4ffa963035479d2.svg" alt="L_{rx}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> between the antenna and the point at which the system noise is referenced — the received carrier power is



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f0bd3482885d29a6.svg" alt="C = \text{EIRP} - \text{FSPL} - L_{atm} - L_{point} - L_{pol} - L_{rx} + G_{RX} \quad \text{(dBW)}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



The noise power spectral density at the same reference point is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_de75d143766a4245.svg" alt="N_0 = k_B T_{sys}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (W/Hz), or in decibels <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2b672a8e25d0b6e9.svg" alt="N_0 = k + 10\log_{10} T_{sys}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0710a82670e6bf6f.svg" alt="k = 10\log_{10}(1.380\,649 \times 10^{-23}) = -228.6" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> dBW/K/Hz. Subtracting, and grouping the receive gain with the noise temperature into the figure of merit <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ef1e7022c090d8c5.svg" alt="G/T = G_{RX} - 10\log_{10} T_{sys}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (dB/K), gives the canonical form of Chapter 11 §11.2:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8f174438743f92e3.svg" alt="\frac{C}{N_0} = \text{EIRP} - \text{FSPL} - L_{atm} - L_{point} - L_{pol} - L_{rx} + G/T - k \quad \text{(dBHz)}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



(Note the sign: subtracting a negative <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7be17d39654538e3.svg" alt="k" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> adds 228.6 dB.) The energy per bit follows by dividing by the bit rate, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5d16a656055715f7.svg" alt="E_b/N_0 = C/N_0 - 10\log_{10} R_b" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, and the required <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4b3eebd564ce5185.svg" alt="E_b/N_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> depends on the modulation and coding (V.8, Figure 11.4). The link margin is



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f599285357809036.svg" alt="\text{Margin} = (E_b/N_0)_{available} - (E_b/N_0)_{required} - L_{impl}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e6bd23c1833a1588.svg" alt="L_{impl}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the modem implementation loss. ECSS-E-ST-50-05C calls for at least 3 dB from Phase B onward; a 6 dB target is common in Phase A while the design is still fluid.

### Verification

The S-band waterfall of Chapter 11 Figure 11.5 (2 W transmitter, 6 dBi patch antenna, 2.25 GHz over 1695 km, 3 m ground dish at 150 K) reads left to right exactly as the equation above: gains add, losses subtract, and the final received <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c2f46c7e8bd57c77.svg" alt="C/N_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> closes at 83.4 dBHz against the 73.0 dBHz required at 5 Mbit/s, leaving the 10.4 dB margin. The EOSat-3U budget of Chapter 11 §11.8.1 is the same calculation line by line (EIRP 7.5 dBW, FSPL 164.1 dB, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3b4348631c46eb35.svg" alt="C/N_0 = 83.4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> dBHz, margin 10.4 dB at 5 Mbit/s).

---

## V.8 — <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4b3eebd564ce5185.svg" alt="E_b/N_0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> versus BER

### Derivation

For coherent BPSK over an additive white Gaussian noise channel, the bit-error probability is



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0f5da94f4cdeeac6.svg" alt="P_b = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}}\right)" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



For QPSK with Gray coding the same expression applies per bit. For 8-PSK:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5fa54baf0380fddd.svg" alt="P_b \approx \frac{2}{3}\, Q\!\left(\sqrt{2 \tfrac{E_b}{N_0}}\, \sin\!\frac{\pi}{8}\right)" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



For non-coherent FSK:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7429e88a697c845d.svg" alt="P_b = \frac{1}{2}\,e^{-E_b/(2 N_0)}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Chapter 11 §11.6 and Figure 11.4 plot these curves together with a representative concatenated (convolutional + Reed–Solomon) coded curve, whose horizontal offset from the uncoded curve at a given BER is the coding gain — about 5 dB at BER <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_72c69b5d571b6785.svg" alt="10^{-5}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> for that scheme, more for LDPC codes.

### Verification

**Sanity check.** BPSK at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3b6ed20c9e537df4.svg" alt="E_b/N_0 = 9.6" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> dB:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_32af9bbaada2fcb0.svg" alt="P_b = 0.5 \times \mathrm{erfc}(\sqrt{10^{0.96}}) = 0.5 \times \mathrm{erfc}(3.02) = 0.5 \times 1.9 \times 10^{-5} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-6}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>.

The standard textbook value is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_72c69b5d571b6785.svg" alt="10^{-5}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at 9.6 dB; the small difference is the resolution of the plot grid.

---

## V.9 — Ground Sample Distance Geometry

### Derivation (diffraction limit)

For an unobstructed circular aperture of diameter <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8dba907f640579f0.svg" alt="D" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, the first minimum of the Airy pattern lies at the half-angle



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a5e73e2bce16c1a7.svg" alt="\theta_{Airy} = 1.22\, \frac{\lambda}{D}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Projected onto the ground at range <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (nadir viewing from altitude <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_739ae27cbb27190f.svg" alt="\text{GSD}_{diff} = \theta_{Airy}\, h = 1.22\, \frac{\lambda\, h}{D}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



### Derivation (pixel limit)

A detector pixel of pitch <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d9be9130ed00d73c.svg" alt="p" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at the focal plane subtends an angle <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8acd54dd913b7d02.svg" alt="p/f" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_564eb7b8172b11af.svg" alt="f" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the focal length. Projected at range <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fadc7bd14aa9f1e9.svg" alt="\text{GSD}_{pix} = \frac{p\, h}{f}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



The achievable GSD is the *larger* of the two — the system cannot resolve better than the optics allow, nor better than the detector samples. Matching the two (so that <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_85ce40ed6e849c8c.svg" alt="p/f \approx 1.22\lambda/D" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, i.e. an f-number of about <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1abf9ba3f631067b.svg" alt="p/(1.22\lambda)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) is the design condition the Payload Lead briefing of Part IV warns about. Off-nadir, replace <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d70b49fc2712c7e6.svg" alt="h" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> by the slant range.

### Verification

Figure D.3 plots both limits against aperture diameter.

![GSD versus aperture diameter — diffraction and pixel limits.](../assets/figures/fig_gsd.png)

**Figure D.3** — Ground sample distance against aperture diameter for visible imagers (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_84c2c9877e0442d1.svg" alt="\lambda = 550" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> nm) at four altitudes, with the diffraction limit as solid curves and the pixel limit at 500 km (6 µm pitch, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0c59f14b7e81d86a.svg" alt="f/D = 5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) as the dashed line. Sentinel-2 heritage at 786 km: the diffraction limit for a 0.135 m aperture is ≈ 3.9 m, consistent with the published 10 m bands once the detector pitch and f-number are accounted for.

**Worked sanity check.** A 3U CubeSat imager with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_458ac62eb23f3c15.svg" alt="D = 90" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> mm at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d864a2c8ff6a310a.svg" alt="h = 500" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7f17f0d793958163.svg" alt="\text{GSD}_{diff} = 1.22 \times 550 \times 10^{-9} \times 5 \times 10^5 / 0.09 = 3.7" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m; with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d1528f2c012993cc.svg" alt="p = 5.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> µm and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4586336477259443.svg" alt="f = 500" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> mm, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e9eecda8f2ff360d.svg" alt="\text{GSD}_{pix} = 5.5 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^5 / 0.5 = 5.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m — pixel-limited, so the achievable GSD is 5.5 m.

---

## V.10 — Radiative Thermal Equilibrium

### Derivation

Energy balance for a flat plate in steady state:

Absorbed = Emitted.
Absorbed = <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ace06f7111c9e9c7.svg" alt="\alpha_s\, S_{eff} + \varepsilon\, \phi_{IR}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (solar input at the orbit-average effective flux <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_93b13d44693a32e5.svg" alt="S_{eff}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, plus the Earth-IR contribution, absorbed at the IR emittance by Kirchhoff's law).
Emitted = <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_54702bcd2fc69320.svg" alt="\varepsilon\, \sigma\, T^4" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> per unit radiating area.

Solving for the equilibrium temperature:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2d09654a7e3c9fb6.svg" alt="T_{eq} = \left(\frac{\alpha_s\, S_{eff} + \varepsilon\, \phi_{IR}}{\sigma\, \varepsilon}\right)^{1/4}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



The ratio <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the dominant design knob. Chapter 9 §9.4 gives the full balance with the albedo term, view factors and internal dissipation, and Figure 9.6 plots <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5c73f1b60030674e.svg" alt="T_{eq}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> against <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> with common coatings marked.

### Verification

**Worked sanity check.** A white-painted radiator, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_784cf6638a1ea811.svg" alt="\alpha_s = 0.15" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ee6804a045b91fa8.svg" alt="\varepsilon = 0.92" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_776a996ade007014.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon = 0.163" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>), one-sided, orbit-averaged at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_735cac4947ee2211.svg" alt="\beta = 0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:

solar: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_52aa98f2311ced3b.svg" alt="S_{eff} \approx 1361/4 = 340" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m², absorbed <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_495ffc659b4d437b.svg" alt="0.15 \times 340 = 51" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m²;
Earth IR: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e00847d60f949b19.svg" alt="\phi_{IR} \approx 230/2 = 115" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m² seen by a nadir-facing plate at LEO, absorbed <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3bab654184bb03e9.svg" alt="0.92 \times 115 = 106" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W/m²;
total absorbed = 157 W/m²;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cc64a3628549007f.svg" alt="T_{eq} = (157 / (0.92 \times 5.670 \times 10^{-8}))^{1/4} = (3.01 \times 10^9)^{1/4} = 234" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> K <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_03d76221db532319.svg" alt="= -39" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> °C.

This matches Figure 9.6 at <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0d529cdb6c319ffa.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon \approx 0.16" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The same balance with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_506b5396c490ef0d.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon \approx 5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (bare polished aluminium) gives roughly +120 °C — the reason bare metal is never left facing the Sun.

## V.11 — Solar Array Sizing

### Derivation

Consider one orbit of period <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_f952139e4fabb558.svg" alt="T = t_{sun} + t_{ecl}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The array generates only during the sunlit arc <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_abfcb95463952c7b.svg" alt="t_{sun}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; the loads run throughout. Let <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_193454029304c366.svg" alt="P_{sun}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> be the peak sunlit-mode demand and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ad43d75ad3da2e37.svg" alt="P_{ecl}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> the eclipse demand. Energy delivered to the loads over the orbit must be supplied by the array, through two paths of different efficiency: the direct array-to-load path in sunlight (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ea65fd7e1b98bc97.svg" alt="\eta_{sun}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, the regulator alone) and the array-to-battery-to-load path for the eclipse energy (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06151b705dffb80c.svg" alt="\eta_{ecl} = \eta_{charge}\,\eta_{discharge}\,\eta_{regulator}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>). The energy balance over one orbit is therefore



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1ca00308784ed1a8.svg" alt="P_{SA,EOL}\, t_{sun} = \frac{P_{sun}\, t_{sun}}{\eta_{sun}} + \frac{P_{ecl}\, t_{ecl}}{\eta_{ecl}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



and, dividing by <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_abfcb95463952c7b.svg" alt="t_{sun}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>,



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ccd6fc2ebb951fa3.svg" alt="P_{SA,EOL} = \frac{\dfrac{P_{sun}\, t_{sun}}{\eta_{sun}} + \dfrac{P_{ecl}\, t_{ecl}}{\eta_{ecl}}}{t_{sun}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



— the array power required at end of life (Chapter 9 §9.2, step 2). The array must deliver this at end of life, so the beginning-of-life rating is higher by the radiation degradation factor <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_772ebfb6a0789499.svg" alt="L_d = (1-\delta)^n" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the temperature derating <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_eb988c0efa4332c0.svg" alt="L_T = 1 + \beta_T (T_{cell} - T_{ref})" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (the cell temperature coefficient is written <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a502447f00f787bb.svg" alt="\beta_T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> to avoid confusion with the orbit <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d231046189335742.svg" alt="\beta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>-angle):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_1d494deb0e66cc21.svg" alt="P_{SA,BOL} = \frac{P_{SA,EOL}}{L_d\, L_T}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Finally the cells convert the solar flux <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0660475a29b87392.svg" alt="S" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at efficiency <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2360dafb58acf75c.svg" alt="\eta_{cell}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, reduced by the cosine of the Sun incidence angle <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6880829b318d5078.svg" alt="\theta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> on the array, the packing factor <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_76767a67bcd4d405.svg" alt="f_{pack}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and the cover-glass transmission <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5132b026a70945df.svg" alt="f_{cover}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4f6994a8d886c895.svg" alt="A_{SA} = \frac{P_{SA,BOL}}{\eta_{cell}\, S\, \cos\theta\, f_{pack}\, f_{cover}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



Here <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_6880829b318d5078.svg" alt="\theta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the angle between the array normal and the Sun vector — zero for a Sun-tracking array; for a body-fixed panel on a nadir-pointed spacecraft it is set by the orbit <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d231046189335742.svg" alt="\beta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>-angle (a panel whose normal is perpendicular to the orbit plane sees <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_516c8517ab07af0d.svg" alt="\theta = 90° - |\beta|" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> constantly; a zenith panel sees <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_07b7ba8d74929329.svg" alt="\cos\theta = \cos\beta\cos\nu" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> varying through the sunlit arc, so its sunlit-arc average is used). Chapter 9 §9.2 states the same chain and works the EOSat-3U numbers.

### Equivalence to the eclipse-fraction form

Many references write the sizing in terms of the eclipse fraction <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0d21a6ee7d86fde6.svg" alt="f_{ecl} = t_{ecl}/T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and sunlit fraction <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4a7e26cb28e84c51.svg" alt="f_{sun} = t_{sun}/T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, with a single orbit-average load <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0b78459d3293ac3c.svg" alt="P_{avg}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and a single degradation factor. Set <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cc8ece6d1bcb3962.svg" alt="P_{sun} = P_{ecl} = P_{avg}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, absorb the sunlit-path efficiency into the load (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_b815c8278915edef.svg" alt="\eta_{sun} \to 1" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>), write <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_36009ad3e9b6e823.svg" alt="\eta_{ecl} \to \eta_{dis}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, and divide numerator and denominator of the first equation by <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_5f8eb8cbe0662591.svg" alt="T" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_03e84a9f384af1b6.svg" alt="P_{SA} = P_{avg}\left(1 + \frac{f_{ecl}}{f_{sun}\, \eta_{dis}}\right)" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



and, with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_180983395418b76a.svg" alt="L_d L_T \to (1 - D_{deg})" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c96c652ed22fc0d7.svg" alt="f_{pack} f_{cover}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> absorbed into <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_2360dafb58acf75c.svg" alt="\eta_{cell}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>,



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d5f71782d94d4325.svg" alt="A_{SA} = \frac{P_{avg}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_{ecl}}{f_{sun}\,\eta_{dis}}\right)}{S\, \eta_{cell}\, \cos\theta\, (1 - D_{deg})}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



The two forms are the same energy balance. The Chapter 9 form is preferred because it separates the peak sunlit mode from the eclipse mode (the array must cover the worst sunlit mode, not the average) and because it keeps the two path efficiencies distinct.

### Verification

The sizing nomograph of Chapter 9 Figure 9.3 is drawn in the eclipse-fraction form (<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c5e3fc9d1f6a8f68.svg" alt="\eta_{cell} = 30" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> %, 10 % EOL degradation, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_708257cc3d024679.svg" alt="\theta = 20°" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_93b9a5700e30fe2e.svg" alt="\eta_{dis} = 85" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> %): a 6U at 15 W orbit-average load needs about 870 cm² at end of life.

**Worked check.** <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a32f5d3a21476801.svg" alt="P_{sun} = P_{ecl} = 15" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a2b12c18a43a7d7b.svg" alt="t_{ecl}/t_{sun} = 0.35/0.65 = 0.538" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_73515d20234ae179.svg" alt="\eta_{sun} = 1" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ab5b80d96d64606a.svg" alt="\eta_{ecl} = 0.85" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_44001ab4cea73b41.svg" alt="P_{SA} = 15 + 15 \times 0.538 / 0.85 = 15 + 9.5 = 24.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W during the sunlit arc;
<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_ff3912f23287cf0e.svg" alt="A_{SA} = 24.5 / (1361 \times 0.30 \times \cos 20° \times 0.90) = 24.5 / 345.0 = 0.071" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m² <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_76fab9231560f60b.svg" alt="= 710" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> cm².

The nomograph reads about 870 cm² because it is drawn for orbit-averaged rather than sunlit-arc generation, the more conservative convention; the two agree to within that modelling choice. The EOSat-3U case of Chapter 9 §9.2 — <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cbd4cf038689df97.svg" alt="P_{sun} = 10" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_255722f29c3b3068.svg" alt="P_{ecl} = 3.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_269fe5bf43d3551b.svg" alt="t_{sun} = 58.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d179dd25f4c89ff5.svg" alt="t_{ecl} = 35.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d8a9da174fcfc2e7.svg" alt="\eta_{sun} = 0.90" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_75fd2f9bf65ed895.svg" alt="\eta_{ecl} = 0.786" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> — gives <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_48caf55e2bc2418a.svg" alt="P_{SA,EOL} = 13.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_83bc51d338d19ffa.svg" alt="P_{SA,BOL} = 16.0" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cbbf191a3b509514.svg" alt="A_{SA} = 0.0526" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m².

---

## V.12 — Battery Sizing

### Derivation

The energy drawn from the battery during one eclipse is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0f1296aba9cc7749.svg" alt="E_{ecl} = P_{ecl}\, t_{ecl}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. The battery must supply this through the discharge path (efficiency <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_716d1d070e1afe23.svg" alt="\eta_{dis}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>) while using only the fraction DoD of its rated capacity, so that it reaches the required cycle life:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8dde8f3487a132fd.svg" alt="E_{bat} = \frac{P_{ecl}\, t_{ecl}}{\text{DoD}\, \eta_{dis}}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



— the form of Chapter 9 §9.3. The rated capacity in ampere-hours is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c9e0aac73d9b2681.svg" alt="C = E_{bat} / V_{bus}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, and the mass follows from the specific energy of the chemistry. The cycle count is the number of eclipses over the mission (≈ 15 per day in LEO, about 5500 per year), which, through the cycle-life-versus-DoD curves of Chapter 9 Figure 9.4, sets the permissible DoD.

### Verification

**Worked check.** EOSat-3U, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_255722f29c3b3068.svg" alt="P_{ecl} = 3.5" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> W, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d179dd25f4c89ff5.svg" alt="t_{ecl} = 35.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> min <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_4204a1c24625e614.svg" alt="= 0.597" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> h, DoD <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_29f05d5eb73348fb.svg" alt="= 25" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> %, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_40bf9e9322389c1f.svg" alt="\eta_{dis} = 0.95" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_236283e6b8a07262.svg" alt="E_{bat} = 3.5 \times 0.597 / (0.25 \times 0.95) = 2.09 / 0.2375 = 8.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> Wh,

as in Chapter 9 §9.3, where the requirement is rounded up with margin and a 20 Wh pack is selected. A three-year mission at 15 eclipses per day is about 16 000 cycles; Figure 9.4 shows that NCA/NMC cells reach this at 25–30 % DoD with margin, whereas heritage LCO cells need a shallower DoD.

---

## V.13 — Margin of Safety (structures)

The structural margin of safety compares the allowable stress with the applied stress multiplied by the factor of safety:



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7feb2bb30fe3bcaf.svg" alt="\text{MoS} = \frac{\sigma_{allow}}{\text{FoS} \cdot \sigma_{applied}} - 1" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



A positive margin is compliant; zero is exactly at the allowable with the factor applied; negative is a failure of the requirement. Chapter 12 §12.1.6 is the canonical treatment (Chapter 3 §3.3.3 and Chapter 14 defer to it) and gives the ECSS-E-ST-32-10C factors.

**Worked check.** Al 7075-T6, yield allowable <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_10f843268cb18250.svg" alt="\sigma_{yield} = 503" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> MPa, yield factor of safety 1.25, applied stress 200 MPa:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9bb144932bc4bbbc.svg" alt="\text{MoS} = 503 / (1.25 \times 200) - 1 = 1.012" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>,

i.e. 100 % positive margin. Compliant. (For the 3U box-beam of Chapter 12 §12.1 the first natural frequency, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_8eca8de1a9aace7d.svg" alt="f_1 \approx 330" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> Hz, is checked separately against the 100 Hz requirement.)

---

## V.14 — Disturbance Torque Order-of-Magnitude

### Derivation (aerodynamic drag)

The drag force on an exposed area <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3e72381368946a57.svg" alt="A_{ref}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a66fcdf898541c74.svg" alt="\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 C_D A_{ref}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>; it acts at the centre of pressure, offset from the centre of mass by a lever arm <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a5ff38b0591a8441.svg" alt="\ell" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, giving the torque



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_c42e1a863e28b051.svg" alt="T_{drag} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\rho\, V^2\, C_D\, A_{ref}\, \ell" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



where <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_30b1cf5c0ff6efc4.svg" alt="\rho" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> is the atmospheric density, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_333ab72f99ea6ee5.svg" alt="V" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> the orbital velocity and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_3529abebbe9f62e3.svg" alt="C_D \approx 2.2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>. Chapter 10 §10.2 gives the companion expressions for gravity gradient, magnetic and solar-pressure torques and the EOSat-3U worked values.

**Worked estimate.** A 6U CubeSat at 500 km, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fd13c84ffbf46cba.svg" alt="\rho \approx 6 \times 10^{-13}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> kg/m³ (mean solar activity), <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_de73bff26aecbc43.svg" alt="V = 7.61" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> km/s, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e5dc2b1435cd48f9.svg" alt="A_{ref} = 0.06" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m², <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_372b4fa6ae9c2a62.svg" alt="C_D = 2.2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e442e5f8d4c1ef37.svg" alt="\ell = 0.02" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> m:

<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_463d423f9a3bed8c.svg" alt="T_{drag} \approx 0.5 \times 6 \times 10^{-13} \times 7610^2 \times 2.2 \times 0.06 \times 0.02 \approx 4.6 \times 10^{-8}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> N m.

With a 10 cm lever arm (a deployed panel far off the centre of mass) the figure is five times larger; across the solar cycle <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_30b1cf5c0ff6efc4.svg" alt="\rho" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> at 500 km varies by more than an order of magnitude either way, which is why Chapter 10 Figure 10.4 shows a band rather than a line.

### Verification

Chapter 10 Figure 10.4 shows the accumulated wheel momentum against orbits since the last desaturation, and the order-of-magnitude disturbance torques by source, for a spacecraft of a few tens of kilograms; the EOSat-3U values of Chapter 10 §10.2 are roughly a tenth of those, and for a 3U at 500 km the magnetic torque, not drag, dominates. The reaction-wheel momentum capacity follows as <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_38a1bb4d511ca2f3.svg" alt="H \ge T_{dist}\, t_{desat}\, k_{margin}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (Chapter 10 §10.3 and §10.5).

---

## V.15 — Daily Data Volume Closure

The closure check between data generation (payload) and downlink capacity (communications) is a classic mission-design failure point. The payload generates <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7e4f50ceb4d7beca.svg" alt="V_{gen} = R_{gen}\, t_{imaging}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> per day; the ground segment can receive, with <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_e3b3d8dbde586041.svg" alt="N_{passes}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> usable passes per day of average usable duration <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_24af2abe0f348273.svg" alt="t_{contact}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>, at data rate <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_cd7836f5693f9a87.svg" alt="R" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> and protocol efficiency <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_7ac0d7a564ba388d.svg" alt="\eta_{protocol}" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> (acknowledgements, framing, re-transmissions):



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_a9a8bd366343c5f4.svg" alt="C_{downlink} = R \cdot N_{passes} \cdot t_{contact} \cdot \eta_{protocol}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



and the mission closes if



<img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_56bd001699e35c68.svg" alt="V_{gen} \le C_{downlink}" class="math-display" style="display:block;margin:8pt auto;"/>



This is the form of Chapter 11 §11.9. If the inequality fails, the options are a faster downlink (more bandwidth or a higher band), more stations or passes, on-board compression, or fewer images. Chapter 11 Figure 11.6 plots daily capacity by band against representative payload volumes: UHF closes only for housekeeping; S-band suits a multispectral imager; X-band is needed for SAR or hyperspectral data.

**Worked check.** EOSat-3U at 5 Mbit/s with four 8-minute passes per day and <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_fe1092bde2a7a42d.svg" alt="\eta_{protocol} = 0.8" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/>: <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_d2fa1541d5f50881.svg" alt="C = 5 \times 10^6 \times 4 \times 480 \times 0.8 / 8 = 960" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> MB/day against 720 MB/day generated — closes (Chapter 11 §11.8 and §11.9 give 956 MB/day with the exact pass durations). UniSat-1 at 4800 bit/s with five minutes of usable contact per pass to a single station: 0.61 MB/day against 1.13 MB/day generated — does not close (Chapter 11 §11.8.2, Chapter 17 §17.6).

## V.16 — Cross-method verification matrix

For a design review, every quantitative claim should be verified by at least two methods. The following matrix lists the two methods expected for each quantity derived in this part.

| Quantity | Method 1 | Method 2 | Derivation |
|----------|---------|---------|--------|
| Orbital period | Kepler (analytical) | Numerical propagation (GMAT or equivalent) | V.2 |
| SSO inclination | Analytical <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_9b3c6c687ea02746.svg" alt="J_2" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> condition | Tabulated (SMAD4 Table 9-2) | V.4 |
| Eclipse fraction | Analytical β-form | Numerical eclipse model | V.5 |
| FSPL | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_38b06b90ab00a68c.svg" alt="20\log_{10}(4\pi d/\lambda)" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | ITU-R P.525 | V.6 |
| Link budget | Spreadsheet, line by line | Concurrent-design tool or vendor link calculator | V.7 |
| GSD (diffraction) | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_0a7c1d58218043a8.svg" alt="1.22\,\lambda h/D" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | Detailed optical ray-trace | V.9 |
| GSD (pixel) | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_302fc9a24a6a3bf2.svg" alt="p\,h/f" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | Detector data sheet | V.9 |
| Thermal equilibrium | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_06dfb77adb6c7125.svg" alt="\alpha_s/\varepsilon" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> analytical | Thermal network model (ESATAN or equivalent) | V.10 |
| Solar-array area | Orbit energy balance | Vendor sizing tool | V.11 |
| Battery capacity | DoD and cycle-life curve | Vendor cycle test data | V.12 |
| Margin of safety | Hand calculation | Finite-element analysis | V.13 |
| Disturbance torque | First-principles estimate | Atmospheric model (NRLMSISE-00) with geometry | V.14 |
| Data budget | <img src="../assets/figures/_math/m_eea69f92f0eb6ead.svg" alt="R\,N_{passes}\,t_{contact}\,\eta" class="math-inline" style="display:inline;vertical-align:middle;"/> | Pass-by-pass simulation with the station schedule | V.15 |
